customers.name: Owners and developers
customers.who: Utilities, independent power producers, hyperscalers, energy and mining companies
customers.need: Choose the right project, commit at a number that holds, and deliver the business case.
pain: Most projects reach execution under-defined: IPA finds only 13% start execution with Good or Best Practical front-end loading, and only those earn a positive IRR.
Stage gates are passed on incomplete evidence, and stakeholders surface problems late.
Every project starts from scratch, and lessons leave with the team.
customers.value: Commit at FID on a number that holds, pass every gate on evidence, and see drift weeks earlier.

tools.name: Opportunity Map
tools.line: See the projects forming in your markets before they reach a tender, ranked by how well they fit.
desc: Opportunity Map watches the signals that come before a capital project is announced: utility resource plans, interconnection queues, permits, land and water rights, financing and offtake. It turns them into a ranked list of projects forming, with the next action for each.

The same view shows whether the market can deliver: contractor backlogs, workforce and equipment lead times. A pursuit that looks attractive but cannot be built on time is flagged before effort is spent on it.

Each opportunity scored against your criteria, with the evidence behind the score

tools.name: Generative Concepts
tools.line: Generates and costs every viable concept for the site and the brief, so the best one is chosen on evidence rather than habit.
desc: Concept Twin generates layouts and quantities from a brief, then builds each concept as a digital twin: equipment, footprint, capital cost, operating cost and lifetime economics. Concepts are compared on the same basis, so the choice rests on evidence rather than on whichever option was studied first.

Assumptions such as fuel price, capacity factor or cooling technology can be changed live, and every concept updates. The chosen concept carries its quantities and costs into the estimate, the schedule and the financial model.
features: Arrangements, equipment lists and quantities generated for engineers to refine
Capital and operating cost for each concept from the cost model
Levelized cost and returns for every option, updated live
Concepts ranked on cost, schedule, risk and returns
Design and contracting alternatives, each priced against the project’s own packages
The concept’s cost per unit of capacity against comparable plants, before it is chosen

Generates layouts and costs every concept for capex, opex and returns

tools.name: Costline
tools.line: Every cost of the project on one traceable line: capital, contingency, escalation, operating, lifecycle and end-of-life.
desc: Cost Model builds estimates bottom-up from quantities and unit rates, using a cost database drawn from completed projects. It produces a should-cost for every package, so bids can be tested line by line against what the work ought to cost.

The same engine gives cost per unit of capacity and levelized cost, and estimates end-of-life cost when an asset is retired. One model replaces the spreadsheets that are usually rebuilt at every stage.

Contingency from quantified risk; escalation and currency by cost index

tools.name: Generative Scheduling
tools.line: A resource-loaded, logic-linked schedule generated from the scope, with durations and crews computed rather than guessed.
desc: Generative Scheduling builds the schedule from the scope rather than from a template. Activities and logic come from the work breakdown and from comparable schedules; durations are computed from quantities, productivity rates and the crews actually available, not typed in. Third-party and permitting activities are modelled explicitly, so their knock-on effect on engineering and construction is visible from the start.

Every activity is linked to elements of the 3D model, so the schedule can be seen as a 4D build. The engine generates alternative sequences, levels resources across projects that share the same people, and runs Monte Carlo simulation on the result to give P50 and P80 dates.
features: Activities and logic from the work breakdown and comparable schedules
Computed from quantities, productivity rates and conditions
Crews, equipment and people across projects, without 100% utilization assumptions
Each activity tied to model elements for the 4D build
Permits, land, utilities and owner deliverables modelled as logic
Monte Carlo P50 and P80 dates

The same twin measures real progress from site imagery, shows system readiness at commissioning, and carries into operations as the as-built model.

desc: RealityScan assembles the record of comparable projects: what they were estimated to cost, what they cost, how late they were and why. It benchmarks a project’s estimate and schedule against that record and shows where it sits.
For assets in operation it benchmarks performance against peers and puts a value on the gap. It is the fastest way to find out whether a number is credible.

tools.name: Outturn Forecast
tools.line: The outside view on cost, schedule and readiness, before capital is committed.
desc: Outturn forecasts final cost and schedule from the outcomes of completed comparable projects, from P5 to P95, and sets contingency at P30, P50 and P80 for the project director, the sponsor and the funders. Only traits supported by evidence can move the number.

Around the forecast it tests everything that decides whether the forecast holds: the estimate method, governance and decision rights, the owner’s team, the commercial strategy and the project’s readiness, with every gap priced. An independent challenge panel closes each finding with a disposition.

tools.name: Cockpit
tools.line: Every project on one screen, with drift flagged before the monthly report.
desc: Cockpit brings every project and programme into one view: cost and dates against the approved case, contingency drawn against progress, and the leading indicators that move first. It flags projects whose spending shape is unlike completed comparables at the same point, in both directions.
When a project drifts, Cockpit prices the recovery options against the cost of a day of delay, so the decision to accelerate is taken on value. Boards receive exceptions, not status.

tools.name: Forensic
tools.line: When a project is in trouble: what happened, why, what it is worth, and how to reset it.
desc: Forensic tests a business case in hours against eight checks on its risk arithmetic, before it reaches a board. When a project is already in difficulty, it reconstructs what happened, tests the root causes and quantifies delay and disruption for claims and disputes.
For projects that need a reset, it sets an independent position with two methods, rebuilds the baseline at a declared confidence and changes the decision rights so the reset holds.

evidence.line: A proprietary evidence base of completed capital projects, collated with their source documents and lessons learned.

opp.happens: The owner scans markets, sites and partners, and decides which opportunities are worth the cost of pursuit.
fail: Pursuits chosen on enthusiasm, not fit

con.happens: Engineers develop alternative development concepts, each with its capex, opex and fundamentals, and the owner chooses which to take forward. IPA finds that only projects reaching Good or Best Practical front-end definition earn a positive IRR, and only 13% of recent projects get there before execution.
deliver: Concept options with capex and opex by region

sel.happens: The chosen concept is tested against comparable outcomes and its risks are quantified.
fail: Unevidenced claims that this project is different

def.happens: Front-end engineering defines the project well enough to commit: scope, estimate, schedule and execution plan.
fail: Estimate class claimed beyond design maturity

fid.happens: The board commits the capital. Everything earlier exists to make this decision sound.
deliver: Outturn forecast at P50 and P80
FID gate pack and board paper

pro.happens: The owner chooses the contracting strategy, runs the tender and awards the work.
fail: Risk allocated to parties that cannot control it

exe.happens: Engineering, procurement and construction run in parallel; the owner manages to the approved case.
fail: Drift seen only in the monthly report

com.happens: Systems are completed, tested and started up, and the asset is handed to operations.

ops.happens: The asset runs; the owner measures it against design and the approved case.

eol.happens: The owner decides whether to extend, repower or retire the asset, and plans the end of its life.

voices.said: Work that sits with third parties is outside our control, and its delays cascade through the engineering deliverables all the way to construction.
Schedules are built as if people work on one project at a time, at full utilization. They do not.
Crew numbers on a project can range from one to six, so fixed durations rarely hold.
Land arrives in batches of parcels, each with its own start date, not all at once.
The owner’s schedule should be informed by the contractors’ level of detail, not kept separate from it.
At several hundred thousand dollars of construction a week, running work in parallel is a deliberate trade of risk for speed.
Cost is tracked per project, not per type of equipment within the project.
The real question is what level of detail tells which story to whom.
A five-year vision is welcome, but the team needs something that delivers value this quarter.
Remapping the data between systems is the hardest part of any change.
